title: Building what’s next for the trades
summary: Procore’s Groundbreak 2026 keynote revealed the real-time margin tracking and voice-first field AI built to give trade contractors their evenings—and their profitability—back.
body_markdown:
At Groundbreak 2026, the Day 1 Product Keynote focused on specialty contractors, with panelists laying out current industry pressures and the tools Procore is building to help trade contractors thrive—including a voice-first mobile app built to bring construction-specific AI to field crews.


### **Key takeaways**


-


**Capacity is the constraint.** Retirement, burnout, and slow payment create a gap that recruiting alone will not close. Contractors need to make sure every worker counts even more.


-


**Specialty contractors are becoming system integrators.** Operational data—rather than reacting to issues outside your control—can now drive strategy from the earliest stages of a project.


-


**Put rates, time, and earned progress in one place.** Contractors should be able to know their profit during the job instead of at closeout.


-


**Keep crews, office, and the GC on the same page.** With Procore Connect and RFI collaboration, all teams are sharing one version of the information.


-


**Let AI start with the records you already keep.** AI agents do the legwork so teams can decide the next steps and make the final call.


### **From labor providers to system integrators**


Sasha Reed, Sr. Director of Customer and Industry Advocacy at Procore, opened with the pressures on the trades, drawing on Procore's report[The Future State of the Specialty Contractor](https://www.procore.com/ebooks/future-state-specialty-contractor-strategic-analysis) .


She said market demand is outpacing contractors' capacity, and that specialty contractors, long the industry's shock absorbers, are now shifting from transactional labor providers to essential system integrators.


Sasha explained:


"We're now at a critical inflection point where your role is starting to shift. You're transforming from transactional labor providers into essential system integrators. That means that your focus is moving from the field to the factory floor.


You're adopting digital platforms. Your practical field use can now be leveraged at the earliest stages of a project. Instead of just showing up to install materials and react to the issues that are most times out of your control, your operational data drives your strategy. It de-risks your schedules, and it can guarantee better outcomes, long-term outcomes.


From our report, we discovered that 41 percent of the construction workforce is set for retirement by 2031. That's only five years away from today. And of the group coming up behind them, only 10 percent are under 25. This is where our capacity limitations are showing up at the most critical points.


But here's what I want you to really pay close attention to: 52 percent of construction workers report that they're experiencing extreme burnout. That's over half of our existing workforce telling us they're experiencing burnout. That's a signal from our workforce that we can't ignore, and we can't wish away.


Even if you hit all of your recruiting benchmarks and goals, you still can't make up the skills gap to meet that demand. Instead, you have to focus on making every single worker you have count more than ever."


**Learn more:**[10 takeaways for the trades from Groundbreak 2026](https://www.procore.com/blog/takeaways-trades-groundbreak-2026)


### **A time entry fix that gave a crew lead his evenings back**


Brian Clark, Director of Product Management at Procore, said he spends his days listening to what is breaking on specialty contractors' jobs.


He described a visit to an early-adopter asphalt and road contractor in the Midwest, whose crew leads were unhappy after Procore launched mobile time entry:


"Now, instead of waiting for a support ticket, we flew out and visited their jobsite. And here's what we found. The tool didn't let the crew leads draft their time offline on site as the day happened. So this one crew lead, after ten hours on the job building roads literally in the middle of nowhere, had to then go home at dinner, spend 30 to 45 minutes entering time and checking his crew's time, then 20 more minutes making sure the mobile app syncs.


Something happened that doesn't often happen when we visit jobsites. This crew lead got emotional. It really got our attention.


Let that sink in for a second. That's not a product complaint. That's a man telling us that our software is standing between him and his kids at the dinner table.


We literally dropped what we were doing, and we immediately started fixing. We built offline draft mode so he could log time on site as the day happened, and then just sync when he got home. We shipped that feature two months later, and that same company now saves every one of their crew leads at least 30 minutes a day.


That is what makes this industry compelling to me. Every fix we make isn't really about the software, it's about having a real impact on someone's life. Like in this case, giving someone back time with their family."


### **Know whether a job is making money while you can still steer**


Brian followed "Bob," a fictional electrical foreman, through a day of planning crews, logging time, pricing a change, and checking his margin. He presented rate tables and production tracking as the first two pieces of an earned value and project controls solution, with the earned percentage sitting next to the hours burned in the budget.


Brian described percent-based forecasting as still to come:


"Your crews know how they're supposed to run their jobs by keeping a handle on real-time cost and how much they've earned, and a forecast they can stand behind. But honestly, nobody can do this in real time at the scale of the jobs we're all running, because the inputs live in three different systems. It's in a spreadsheet. It's a gut feel for percent complete, and you manually build forecasts. Your project management and cost management tools have not matched how you actually bill on unit-based contracts.


Think about your last job for a second. Be honest. Did you know in real time exactly how profitable it was? Or did you find out two weeks later, or worse, at closeout?


Until now, those rates have lived in spreadsheets, printed union agreements, and unfortunately, in somebody's memory, keyed in by hand on every ticket and every change order.


You felt this pain. You define the resources and rates once, cost and billable, by classification, by equipment type, with effective dates and including project-level overrides, so a foreman can adjust on one job without breaking everything else.


Now here's what that unlocks. Where work gets priced, the dollars fill in automatically, and timesheet hours hit the rate tables directly.


A T&M ticket flows into a change event already priced and onto the change order with rates attached. No rekeying and no separate spreadsheets that somebody has to reconcile at month end. You set the rate once and it travels with the work all the way to your P&L.


Production tracking used to mean logging a percentage that felt about right. I think we're about 20 percent done. We're replacing that with rules of credit and components, leading to claiming schemes that credit partially complete work against real units installed with labor hours, and not a single gut-filled number. \[…\] You take a run of pipe: you lay it out, you weld it, test it, insulate it. Each step has a distinct defined value agreed on before the job ever started. So when your crew logs the weld is done, that's not an opinion. It's a percentage everybody signed off on in advance."


### **AI that keeps expertise working as the workforce shrinks**


Miles Gordenker, Senior Director, Applied AI at Procore, closed the keynote with Procore AI as a digital coworker for specialty contractors, tied to the workforce numbers Sasha had cited.


He described a Starter Pack of five agents, Agent Studio for building your own, and a voice-first mobile app for the jobsite:


"Procore AI is a digital coworker built for the real-world complexity of projects. A single construction project generates an enormous, interconnected web of drawings, specs, RFIs, and submittals, far more than any one person can hold in their head. Your team shouldn't have to dig through all of it by hand, hoping to piece together a useful answer.


Procore AI is one way we help close that gap, not by replacing your best people's judgment, but by capturing it so it keeps working for your team, even as that headcount shrinks."


For the jobsite itself, the Daily Log Agent combines voice notes with photos to create a comprehensive log, so the whole project runs smoother because it has accurate data, and the site safety agent finds these subtle patterns by analyzing many safety records and photos all at once, giving your team a chance to intervene before an incident. At each step, the agents are doing all that tedious legwork, freeing your team up to decide the right next steps and make that final call.


And because not everyone on your crew is sitting at a laptop, nor should they have to be, we're bringing this same intelligence to Procore AI Go. It's a voice-first mobile app built for the jobsite, not the office. No tablet, no typing, no fighting that harness to pull up an answer. Your team asks out loud over the noise of an active site and you get a real answer back."
